name: Coffee enema

lead: A coffee enema is a practice in alternative medicine in which brewed coffee solution is introduced into the rectum and held briefly, with the aim of cleansing the colon and supporting the liver. Followers also say it brings clearer skin, energy and regularity, which is how it reaches appearance discussion.
It grew out of early twentieth-century German medicine and became widely known through Max Gerson's therapy. Research has not confirmed the detox claims, and case reports describe serious harms.

paras: The practice is self-administered with an enema kit and warm coffee, typically using filtered water, and it is used in some wellness and bodybuilding circles as a detox step.

Case reports describe rectal burns from hot liquid, proctocolitis and acute colitis, and electrolyte disturbances, with deaths in the medical literature; a systematic review of case reports concluded evidence on effectiveness and safety is rare.[1][2][3][4][5]

angle.text: Followers describe coffee enemas as a way to clear the body of waste and support the liver, with clearer skin among the reported benefits; research has not confirmed these.

lead: A coffee enema is an alternative-medicine procedure in which brewed coffee is introduced into the rectum and retained for a short period, promoted as a way to detoxify the colon and liver.[1] It is a central part of the Gerson therapy, developed by the German-born physician Max Gerson (1881 to 1959), who promoted a diet-based cancer regimen from 1928.[2]

Proponents say that coffee compounds such as cafestol palmitate increase activity of the enzyme glutathione S-transferase and stimulate bile excretion, and they also cite benefits for constipation, immunity, migraines and clearer skin; wellness influencers have popularised it on social media.[1][1] In bodybuilding forums it is mentioned as liver support or a morning ritual.

Research includes a small crossover trial in healthy volunteers that found no improvement in blood antioxidant markers, pharmacokinetic work on caffeine absorption, and a pilot trial in capsule endoscopy preparation.[3][4][5] Case reports describe burns and colitis, and the National Cancer Institute and American Cancer Society have said Gerson therapy has not been shown to benefit patients.[2][6]

paras: The practice uses a coffee solution cooled to body temperature in an enema kit and held in the lower bowel for a short time. It differs from conventional medical enemas, which use saline or similar solutions for evacuation or procedure preparation.[1] Colon-cleansing in general draws on the older idea of autointoxication, coined in 1884 by Charles Jacques Bouchard, which was rejected by mainstream medicine in the early twentieth century and resurged in the 1990s.[6]

Proponents claim liver detoxification, bile-duct dilation, relief of constipation, immune support and relief of conditions such as migraines and allergies; influencer testimonials mention vitality and clearer skin.[1][1]

The American Cancer Society states available evidence does not support colon therapy for cancer or other disease, and the FDA regulates colon hydrotherapy equipment but not its use and has issued warning letters over false claims.[6] The NCI found no evidence of benefit from Gerson therapy and no independent reproduction of its results.[2]

Case reports describe proctocolitis, acute colitis with abdominal pain and bleeding, and rectal burns from hot coffee.[7][8][9][10] Gerson-related coffee enemas have contributed to at least three US deaths, and a 1980 JAMA paper reported deaths related to coffee enemas; electrolyte disturbance, dehydration and infection have been documented.[2][6]

A systematic review of case reports on self-administered coffee enema aimed to assess safety and effectiveness and noted evidence is rare.[11] In an open-label crossover trial of 11 healthy Thai men, neither coffee enemas nor oral coffee improved serum glutathione or reduced malondialdehyde, and total antioxidant capacity fell.[3] A pharmacokinetic crossover in 11 men compared caffeine after 500 mL coffee enema versus oral coffee.[4] A pilot of 34 patients found coffee enema plus PEG did not differ for proximal small-bowel preparation for capsule endoscopy, with a tendency to better mid and distal preparation and no complications.[5]
